issues.legal_issue: A prosecution sanction is valid for an offence when the sanctioning authority considered facts that support that offence, even if another offence included in the sanction is not ultimately proved.
material_facts: The sanction described the official’s entrustment with the standing crops, his allowing the crops to be cut, and his failure to deposit the proceeds into government funds.

The sanction expressly referred to the offence of dishonest or fraudulent misappropriation or conversion of entrusted property, and evidence showed that the sanctioning authority had considered the relevant materials.
The official was convicted of the entrusted-property offence but acquitted of the separate offence of obtaining a pecuniary advantage.
issues.conclusion: The sanction was sufficient to support prosecution and conviction for the entrusted-property offence despite the acquittal on the separate charge.
issues.legal_principle: A valid sanction must relate to the facts constituting the offence charged. Those facts should appear in the sanction, but if they do not, the prosecution may establish by other evidence that they were placed before the sanctioning authority. The facts considered must be correlated with the particular offence charged. The Court applied Section 6(1)(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and relied on Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King and Jaswant Singh v. The State of Punjab.

rule.if: corruption_prosecution_appeal and sanction_facts_disclosed_or_proved and sanction_authority_considered_facts and facts_support_charged_offense

predicates.corruption_prosecution_appeal: The case is an appeal in a prosecution alleging misconduct by a public official.
predicates.sanction_facts_disclosed_or_proved: The facts supporting the charged offence appear in the sanction or are proved to have been placed before the sanctioning authority.
predicates.sanction_authority_considered_facts: The sanctioning authority considered the relevant facts before authorizing prosecution.
predicates.facts_support_charged_offense: The facts considered by the authority support the particular offence for which prosecution is pursued.

issues.definition: When a corruption-prosecution appeal involves a sanction based on facts considered by the authority that support the charged offence, the sanction is valid for that offence.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s prior written statement may be used to contradict the witness only after the witness’s attention is drawn to the relevant part, and it is not substantive evidence of the facts stated.
material_facts: Some witnesses had signed statements previously recorded by military authorities.
The Court considered whether those statements could be used without confronting the witnesses with the relevant passages during their testimony.
issues.conclusion: A prior statement may be used to contradict a witness only in the manner prescribed by the Evidence Act; the relevant passage must be put to the witness, and the statement is not substantive evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 145 of the Evidence Act governs contradiction by a prior written statement: the witness’s attention must be drawn to the specific part relied upon. A statement used in that way is considered with the witness’s testimony in assessing credibility, but the whole statement is not substantive evidence.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial or an appeal arising from one.
predicates.prior_writing_used_to_contradict_witness: A party relies on a witness’s earlier written statement to challenge the witness’s testimony.
predicates.attention_called_to_relevant_passage: The witness is directed to the specific passage in the earlier writing relied upon for contradiction.

issues.definition: In a criminal trial, a prior writing relied on to contradict a witness may be considered for that purpose, but not as substantive evidence, when the witness’s attention has been drawn to the relevant passage.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for dishonest or fraudulent dealing with property entrusted to a public official may be sustained when the official allows another person to take the property without accounting for it, and the evidence supports the concurrent findings of guilt.
material_facts: The official took possession of land on which standing crops remained and was responsible for the work involving that land.

The evidence supported findings that the crops remained on the land after the official took possession, that delivery of the land to the contractor was delayed, and that the crops were cut and taken away during that period.
The official did not account for the crops or their value and denied that crops were standing, despite documentary evidence to the contrary.
The trial court convicted the official and the High Court affirmed the conviction.
issues.conclusion: The evidence established that the official was entrusted with the crops and dishonestly or fraudulently allowed them to be taken without accounting for them; the concurrent conviction was therefore upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, covers a public servant who dishonestly or fraudulently misappropriates or converts entrusted property, or allows another person to do so; Section 5(2) provides the punishment. The Court also stated that it does not ordinarily reappreciate evidence as a court of fact or disturb concurrent findings of the trial court and High Court absent justification.

rule.if: appeal_against_conviction and public_official_entrusted_with_property and official_dishonestly_allowed_another_to_take_property and property_not_accounted_for and concurrent_findings_supported_by_evidence

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal against a criminal conviction.
predicates.public_official_entrusted_with_property: A public official received or controlled property in the course of official duties.
predicates.official_dishonestly_allowed_another_to_: The official dishonestly or fraudulently permitted another person to take or convert the property.
predicates.property_not_accounted_for: The official did not account for the property or its proceeds.
predicates.concurrent_findings_supported_by_evidenc: The trial court and appellate court reached the same finding of guilt, and the evidence supports that finding.

issues.definition: When an appeal against conviction concerns entrusted property that a public official dishonestly allowed another to take without accounting for it, and supported concurrent findings establish those facts, the conviction is sustained.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction is not invalidated because relied-on circumstances were not put to the accused when the circumstances forming the basis of conviction were put to the accused during examination.
material_facts: The accused challenged reliance on documents and circumstances that he said had not been put to him.
During examination under the applicable criminal procedure, the accused was asked about the possession of the land, the crops, the contractor’s evidence, and the relevant letter concerning the crops.
The Court found that the circumstances forming the basis of the conviction had been put to the accused.
issues.conclusion: The conviction was not invalidated on the ground that the circumstances relied on had not been put to the accused.
issues.legal_principle: The accused must be given an opportunity during examination under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, to address the circumstances relied on against him. The Court found that the material circumstances underlying this conviction had been put to the accused.

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a criminal conviction.
predicates.circumstances_forming_basis_of_convictio: The accused was questioned about the circumstances that form the basis of the conviction.

issues.definition: In a criminal conviction appeal, putting the circumstances forming the basis of conviction to the accused means the conviction is not invalidated for failure to put those circumstances.

issues.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to call additional witnesses or produce a requested record does not by itself defeat the case when the material facts are established by other evidence and the omission causes no demonstrated defect.
material_facts: The accused argued that additional witnesses should have been called and that a requested register had not been produced.
The Court found that examined witnesses provided evidence concerning the matters for which the additional witnesses were said to be necessary, including the relevant possession receipt.
The trial and appellate courts had assessed the oral and documentary evidence and found the charge proved.
issues.conclusion: The omissions did not constitute a defect in the prosecution case or justify setting aside the conviction.
issues.legal_principle: The failure to call additional witnesses is not a defect merely because they might have been called where the relevant matter is already covered by other evidence. The Court found no basis to treat the missing witnesses or record as prejudicial in light of the evidence presented.

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a criminal conviction.
predicates.additional_witnesses_or_record_not_produ: The prosecution did not call additional proposed witnesses or produce a requested record.
predicates.material_facts_established_by_other_evid: Other evidence presented in the case established the material facts for which the omitted evidence was sought.

issues.definition: In a criminal conviction appeal, when material facts are established by other evidence, the nonproduction of additional witnesses or a requested record does not defeat the prosecution case.
